title: Tenant isolation and demand surge playbook (PRD draft)
body:
Purpose and scope

This is a pragmatic PRD-style playbook focused on how Dedicated customers are guaranteed isolation during normal traffic and during short-term demand surges. It combines product requirements (customer-facing controls and SLAs), runtime design options (hard vs soft isolation, preemption, and surge credits), and operator/runbook guidance for incidents. The intent is to produce a minimal viable feature set that can ship within two quarters and then iteratively grow toward full QoS lanes and contractual guarantees.

Problem statement

Customers running Redwood Dedicated need predictable tail latency and throughput even when noisy tenants spike. Existing reserved capacity allocation protects steady-state throughput but lacks affordable, controllable ramping for real application traffic patterns (e.g., short bursts due to marketing events, holiday spikes, model evaluation runs). Without additional controls we observe two failure modes:
- Noisy-burst interference: a tenant suddenly consumes capacity leading to other tenants' latency violations.
- Hard throttling or evictions: aggressive preemption leads to poor customer experience during temporary bursts.

Goals (measurable)

1) Isolation guarantees: maintain p99 generation latency <= contract SLO for 95% of customers under median burst scenarios (define med-burst later).
2) Controlled burst: enable each tenant to consume an additional X% of their committed throughput for short windows (configurable; default 20% for 5 minutes) without impacting neighbors beyond defined QoS tiers.
3) Predictable billing and reconciliation: surfacing burst consumption and automatic application of surge credits or metered overage in billing exports.
4) Operational simplicity: shipping with a single new control-plane API and minimal runtime kernel changes; avoid migration friction for current customers.

Non-goals

- Replacing Dedicated architecture or implementing full hardware partitioning (MIG-level per-tenant GPUs) in the first release.
- Supporting unbounded shared-hosted bursting for all tenants—this is about bounded, contract-safe surges.

Key actors and personas

- Platform engineer (operator): configures global surge windows, quota pools, and emergency limits.
- Customer SRE/Dev: sets tenant burst profile, surge policy, and preferred fallback.
- Billing team: maps burst consumption to invoices and surge credits.
- Runtime engineer: implements admission policies and graceful degradation.

User stories

- As a customer SRE, I want a per-tenant burst profile so my product can absorb short traffic spikes without manual intervention.
- As an operator, I want to enforce tenant isolation so one tenant's spike cannot push others over their latency SLO.
- As an account manager, I want usage exports that show burst minutes and tokens consumed so billing is auditable.

Proposed model (high level)

We propose a two-tiered approach: soft burst credits + hard isolation lanes.

1) Soft burst credits (burst wallet)
- Each tenant has a configurable burst wallet expressed as "burst units". A default allocation (e.g., 20 units per 100 reserved units) allows short surges.
- Burst units deplete while the tenant consumes above their reserved baseline and replenish slowly over time (token bucket-like refill at account-configurable rate).
- Using burst units does not preempt other tenants; instead, low-priority work in the shared pool is rate limited to accommodate bursts within capacity headroom.

2) Hard isolation lanes (isolation lanes)
- Cluster nodes expose explicit lanes: reserved-lane (guaranteed), best-effort-lane (shared), and surge-lane (time-limited, prioritized for tenants with burst budget).
- Isolation lanes are implemented via request routing + scheduler constraints. When surge-lane is exhausted or unsafe, traffic falls back to best-effort with explicit throttling/failover strategies.

Admission and fallback policies

- Admission checks: at request arrival, evaluate tenant's current baseline allocation, burst wallet, current node utilization, and global surge policy.
- If admission would violate neighbor SLOs (estimated by p99 model and current load), reject or queue requests according to tenant's configured fallback: queue (short wait), degrade model (lower-cost quantized variant), or reject with 429.
- Graceful degradation: prefer model downgrade + prioritization over immediate reject where possible. Provide SDK-friendly error codes that signal fallback reason and suggested retry-after.

Runtime design considerations

- Isolation primitives: start with runtime-level scheduling and token accounting (no immediate kernel changes). Use request prioritization, weight-based scheduling, and soft cgroup-like token buckets for GPU memory and compute share.
- Node-level enforcement: implement admission controller in front of the inference runtime to avoid overcommitting GPU kernels that would evict KV caches.
- KV cache / prefix caching: treat cache occupancy as part of admission heuristics; prefer bursts to hit cached keys to lower marginal cost.

Configuration surface (customer-facing)

- burst_profile: {"burst_pct": "20", "window_minutes": "5", "refill_minutes": "30", "mode": "auto|manual"} (document style example in UI)
- fallback_policy: one of ["model-downgrade", "queue", "reject"], plus queue_max_ms and downgrade_model_id
- isolation_tier: one of ["gold", "silver", "bronze"] used to map customers into lane priorities

Billing and contract mapping

- Burst consumption is recorded as burst_units and exported every 5m to billing. Default commercial model: first N burst_units per billing cycle are included as a soft credit depending on contract tier; additional are metered at configurable overage rate.
- Provide near-realtime billing alerts when burst credit consumption hits 75/90/100% so customers can act.

SLOs and success metrics

- Platform: under simulated medium burst across 10% of tenants, <=5% tenants see p99 violations beyond SLA.
- Customer-facing: 95% of requests that use burst wallet complete within baseline p95 latency + 50ms.
- Financial: average overage revenue from burst should be <8% of Dedicated revenue first year (conservative expectation).

Operational runbook (incident flows)

1) Detection
- Alerts when cluster-wide node saturation > 85% or when eviction counts spike. Alerts when more than X tenants hit >90% burst use.

2) Triage
- Query: which tenants are consuming bursts, which models & routes, and whether KV cache hit rates changed.
- Decide: apply emergency limits (global surge cap), or temporarily increase cluster capacity (if autoscaling allowed).

3) Mitigation options (ordered)
- Apply per-tenant emergency throttle (reduce burst_limit to 0) for top hitters.
- Switch some tenants to predefined downgrade models via policy.
- Spin up dedicated warm-pool nodes to absorb short surges (if capacity available).

4) Postmortem signals
- Capture root cause (traffic pattern or client misconfiguration), billing impact, and recommended policy changes.

Rollout plan and phases

Phase 0 (Q1): API & metrics only
- Implement control-plane APIs to set burst_profile and fallback_policy; surface metrics for burst_units. No runtime enforcement yet (simulated limits + monitoring).

Phase 1 (Q2): Soft burst wallet + basic admission controller
- Runtime admission that deducts burst_units and enforces soft limits in cluster. Default fallback -> model-downgrade. Small group of opt-in customers.

Phase 2 (Q3): Isolation lanes + billing integration
- Implement lane routing and queueing. Integrate with billing exports and surge credits. Wider beta.

Phase 3 (Q4+): Smart predictive warm pools + contract SLAs
- Predictive autoscaler integration, contract-level surge SLAs, and advanced QoS (MIG integration exploration if feasible).

Open questions and risks

- Headroom estimation: how to safely compute neighbor impact without overly conservative estimates that block legitimate bursts? Need a simulator and offline experiments.
- Billing complexity: ensuring burst accounting is auditable and understandable to customers.
- Hardware constraints: GPUs with large models and high KV-cache pressure are less tolerant of bursty preemption. This may require per-model profiles.

Implementation notes and TODOs

- TODO: Define burst_units to tokens conversion (ops: tokens consumed vs compute-weighted units) — owner: serving-runtime (JIRA DED-1292).
- TODO: Small simulator that runs synthetic 1000-tenant bursts to validate admission controller heuristics — owner: applied-ml team.
- TODO: UX: compact burst dashboard in Console with 3-tier view (tenant, cluster, org) — owner: devex.

Appendix: Example customer configuration (text)

Customer A (ecommerce scale):
- reserved_throughput: 100 rps baseline
- burst_profile: burst_pct=30, window_minutes=10, refill_minutes=60, mode=auto
- fallback_policy: model-downgrade (to quant-8 variant)

Expected behavior: during a 7-minute traffic spike to 300 rps, Customer A will consume burst wallet; runtime will admit excess requests into surge-lane as long as cluster headroom and neighbor SLOs are safe; otherwise requests will be served with the quant-8 variant or queued up to queue_max_ms before 429.

Notes to reviewers

- This PRD is intentionally pragmatic — prefer shipping a small set of safe defaults and iterating. Feedback wanted on burst wallet economics and how conservative the default burst_pct should be.
- Please add experimental ideas or edge cases as comments below; mark anything that must be in the first release.

End of draft
